पद्म: Padma1 m.: A mythical serpent, also called Padmanābha, 12. 343. 4; 12. 349. 5. A. Birth: Son of Surasā, hence सौर-सेय 12. 348. 3 (identical with one of the two Padmas2 ?); his noble family pure like the water of Ganges 12. 343. 11. B. Residence: His abode (नागायतन, पन्नगालय 12. 345. 3, 7) at *Nāgapura (नागाह्वयं पुरम्) on the river Gomatī in the Nai-miṣa (forest) 12. 343. 2. C. Qualities: Great (महान्), righteous (धर्मात्मा) 12. 343. 4; intelligent and proficient in the शास्त्रस् (बुद्धिशास्त्रविशारदः) 12. 343. 8; endowed with all excellent qualities 12. 343. 8-10; Padma himself described the नागस् to be of great prowess, speedy, and guardians of the wealth of human beings (मनुष्याणां विशेषेण धनाध्यक्षा इति श्रुतिः) 12. 348. 3-4. D. Conduct: Pleased all beings with his speech, action and thought 12. 343. 5; employed four means सामन्, दान, दण्ड, and भेद against his opponents, and protected his own people with his attentive eye (?) 12. 343. 6 (चक्षुर्-ध्यानेन रक्षति। But Nī. चक्षुरादिध्या-नेन वस्तुतत्त्वानुसन्धानेन on 12. 355. 6 Bom. Ed.); by nature, pure like water (?प्रकृत्या नित्यसलिलः on which Nī. नित्यं सलिलवन् निर्मलः नित्यसलिलः 12. 355. 9 Bom. Ed.). E. Epithets: As a serpent, called चक्षुःश्रवस् ‘whose eye is his ear’ 12. 343. 4, दर्शनश्रवस् 12. 347. 16, and अनिलाशन ‘who lives on air’ 12. 348. 5. F. Status: Chief among the serpents (भुजगेन्द्र 12. 344. 10; नागेन्द्र 12. 347. 7, 15; 12. 349. 2), the best among the ser-pents (उत्तमनाग 12. 345. 6; भुजगत्तम 12. 347. 15; भुजगसत्तम 12. 352. 2; उरगश्रेष्ठ 12. 353. 1; द्विजश्रेष्ठ 12. 349. 5); king of serpents (पन्नगपति 12. 349. 1; भोगपति 12. 352. 9; भुजगपति 12. 353. 9). G. Wife and Relatives: His wife, not named (नागपत्नी 12. 345. 4, नागी 12. 345. 13), virtuous and devoted; she knew what the duties of a student and a servant were, was familiar with the duties of the four वर्णस्, and knew the duties of a householder and his wife; she had learnt these from her husband Padma; she therefore made no mistake in receiving the guests during the absence of her husband; on a certain occasion she duly received and honoured a Brāhmaṇa who arrived at Padma's residence 12. 345. 4-12; when Padma arrived she informed him about the arrival of a Brāhmaṇa who wanted to meet him and had taken his residence on the river Gomatī; she advised Padma to see the Brāhmaṇa 12. 347. 13-16; Padma's sense of pride was hurt since he was commanded by a Brāhmaṇa to go and meet him; he there-fore asked his wife whether the Brāhmaṇa was really a human being or a god in disguise 12. 348. 1-2; his wife told him that she did not consider the Brāhmaṇa to be a god (in dis-guise); she advised her husband to give up his inborn anger (तद् रोषं सहजं त्यक्त्वा 12. 348. 8) and go and meet the Brāhmaṇa 12. 348. 5-8; Padma realized that he was too proud, that being the fault of his species (जातिदोष 12. 348. 13), and was happy that his wife had burnt his anger by her admoni-tion (दग्धो वाचाग्निना त्वया 12. 348. 13); he felt himself praiseworthy to have such a virtuous wife 12. 348. 13-14, 18-19; during Padma's absence his relatives—brothers, sons and wife—had gone to the river Gomatī to persuade the Brāhmaṇa who almost starved himself to take some food but he did not; they returned home without achieving their purpose 12. 346. 1-13. H. Padma's functions: It was his duty to pull by rotation the sun's one-wheeled chariot for a month (in a year ?) (सूर्यरथं वोढुं गतोऽसौ मासचारिकः 12. 345. 8; विवस्वतो गच्छति पर्ययेण वोढुं भवांस् तं रथम् एकचक्रम् 12. 350. 1). I. Padma and the Brāhmaṇa Dharmāraṇya (12. 349. 5): Padma returned home after he had performed his duty of drawing the Sun's cha-riot and was permitted by the god to leave; he was then informed by his wife about the arrival of a Brāhmaṇa; she informed Padma that the Brāhmaṇa had asked him to meet him; Padma's initial reaction, due to his sense of pride, was not to oblige the Brāhmaṇa; but on the advice of his wife he relented and met the Brāhmaṇa; he then told his wife that he realized that it was not in one's interest to get angry for in bygone days, Rāvaṇa, Kārtavīrya and his sons were killed due to their anger 12. 348. 13-17; he appro-ached the Brāhmaṇa Dharmāraṇya and asked him what he wanted 12. 349. 3-4, 9-12; the Brāhmaṇa first asked Padma a question; after hearing Padma's answer, the Brāhmaṇa would tell Padma the purpose of his visit 12. 349. 16; the Brāhmaṇa asked Padma to tell him if while pulling the god Sun's chariot. he saw anything wonderful on his way 12. 350. 1; Padma first told the Brāhmaṇa that there was nothing more wonderful than the Sun himself (accomplished sages and deities resort to his rays; wind resorts to sun's rays and flows from there to fill the sky; rain water is released by his dark foot (ray ?), Śukra by name, (शुक्रो नामासितः पादो यस्य वारिधरो ऽम्बरे । तोयं सृजति वर्षासु 12. 350. 4); Sun takes back the rain water with his shining ray during eight months; the soul (आत्मा) is for all times established in his lustre; he is the seed of everything, movable and immovable and the earth is sustained by him; the long-armed, eternal, unalterable god having no beginning and no end resides in the sun 12. 350. 2-7); Padma next told him that one day something unusual happened: while the Sun was shining brightly at mid-day, there suddenly appeared light in all directions, light similar to that of the sun; then, as if tearing open the sky a being, looking like a second Sun (द्वितीय इव भास्करः 12. 350. 11), appro-ached the Sun; the Sun held out his hand to receive him and the other being also extended his right hand to hold the Sun's hand; then the being entered the Sun's disc 12. 350. 8-15; confused as to who was the real Sun—the one in the chariot or the one that arrived from the sky—Padma and others asked the Sun to explain; the Sun told them that the one who entered him was a sage who observed the vow of उञ्छवृत्ति (living only on grains fallen in the field); the sage also lived successively on fruit, roots, fallen leaves, water and air and recited the ऋच् stanzas; that Brāhmaṇa (sage) even now moved round the earth with the Sun —this was the wonder seen by Padma 12. 351. 1-6; the Brāhmaṇa Dharmāraṇya, on hearing Padma's account, took leave of him without telling him the purpose of his visit; to the perplexed Padma, Dharmāraṇya explained that he was only curious to know what led to the accumulation of merit (पुण्यसंचय); now that he knew how one did it, he had decided to observe उञ्छव्रत; the purpose of his visit was served (कृतार्थो ऽस्मि) and hence he was leaving 12. 352. 1-10.

Padma2 m.: (du.) Two mythical serpents having the same name (द्वौ पद्मौ) living in Bhogavatī Purī 5. 101. 13. 1. Sons of Surasā and Kaśyapa 5. 101. 4, 17; description 5. 101. 5-7; the two also listed by Sūta among the sons of Kadrū (द्वौ च पद्माव् इति) 1. 31. 10, 2; one of them waits, without feeling fatigue, on Varuṇa in his सभा; marked with banner (पताकिन्) and round spots (मण्डलिन्), hooded (फण-वन्त्) 2. 9. 8, 10, 11.

Padma m.: Name of a particular arrangement of the army (व्यूह). It was arranged by Droṇa in the in-terior of, and in the rear portion of, the principal व्यूह called Cakraśakaṭa; Padma was considered extremely impenetrable (पश्च्-आर्धे तस्य पद्मस् तु गर्भव्यूहः सुदुर्भिदः) 7. 63. 23; in addition, inside the Padma was arranged a concealed (गूढ) व्यूह called Sūcī. [See Cakra-śakaṭa].
पद्मकेसर: Padmakesara m.: A mythical bird, living in the world of Suparṇas 5. 99. 11, 1. Born in the कुल of Vainateya (Garuḍa), in the वंश of Kaśyapa; feeding on serpents; marked with श्रीवत्स, his deity is Viṣṇu; by action a Kṣatriya not obtaining Brahminhood because engaged in destroying his kinsmen 5. 99. 2-8.
पनस: Panasa m.: A monkey-chief. Described as intelligent and very strong; he came to assist Rāma with fifty seven crores of monkeys 3. 267. 6; fought a duel with the demon Paṭuśa 3. 269. 8; he was eaten up by Kumbhakarṇa 3. 271. 4.
पराशर: Parāśara m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya; described as ‘fast as wind’ (वातवेग) and ‘having excess of poison’ (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 17, 13.
परिबर्ह: Paribarha m.: A mythical bird, living in the world of Suparṇas 5. 99. 13, 1. Born in the कुल of Vainateya (Garuḍa), in the वंश of Kaśyapa; feeding on serpents; marked with श्रीवत्स, his deity is Viṣṇu; by action a Kṣatriya not obtaining Brahminhood because engaged in destroying his kinsmen 5. 99. 2-8.
पलित: Palita m.: A mouse. A. Recidence: Lived in a hole, having hundred outlets, at the foot of a banyan tree 12. 136. 21. B. Qualities: He was very wise, intelligent, thoughtful, versed in scriptures, knew how things shaped them-selves, and the proper time for conciliation and feud (प्राज्ञ 12. 136. 191; प्रज्ञावन्त् 12. 136. 192; महाप्राज्ञ 12. 136. 21, 26. 100; मतिमन्त् 12. 136. 87; बुद्धिसंमत and शास्त्रविद् 12. 136. 100; शास्त्रार्थतत्त्वज्ञ 12. 136. 191; धर्मतत्त्वज्ञ 12. 136. 181; परमार्थज्ञ 12. 136. 128; अर्थगति-तत्त्वज्ञ and सन्धिविग्रहकालविद् 12. 136. 47); according to the cat Lomaśa Palita was Uśanas himself in intelligence 12. 136. 127. C. Palita-Lomaśa Episode: Once when the cat Lomaśa who lived on the branches of the same banyan tree was caught in the trap (उन्माथ) fixed by a Cāṇḍāla, Palita moved about fearlessly; he got a piece of flesh and as he was eating it after taking it on the top of the trap and smiling mentally (मनसा हसन् 12. 136. 28) at his enemy, trapped below, Palita saw his second enemy, a mongoose by name Harika, approaching the tree and looking up at his prey; Palita at that moment, also saw a third enemy, an owl named Candraka, prowling from his nest situated on the branch of the same tree; apprehending danger from both directions, Palita decided to take help from the cat, his foe in distress, and find escape from all the three 12. 136. 26-42; he therefore addressed himself to the cat pointing out that there was danger to the life of both of them, that both lived on the same tree and therefore deserved to be friends of each other on the basis of common residence (सवासो मे ऽसि पण्डितः व्ल्। पण्डित 12. 136. 54), that he was prepared to cut the cords that bound the cat provided the cat agreed not to kill him when freed; Palita appealed to the cat: “I wish you live, and you should wish that I live” 12. 136. 48-62; the cat agreed to the proposal and asked Palita to do what was suited to the occasion; Palita swore by truth (सत्येन ते शपे 12. 136. 73) to cut down the net pro-vided the cat agreed not to kill him when he descended and crawled very close to the body of the cat (अहं त्वानुप्रवेक्ष्यामि 12. 136. 72); when the cat agreed to this, Palita went near the cat and rested quietly on his chest; seeing him safe, the mongoose and the owl returned to their residence 12. 136. 66-82; Palita then started to cut slowly the cords of the net; when the cat asked Palita to finish the work quickly, Palita advised him to be patient; Palita would complete cutting the net only when he saw the Caṇḍāla, who had spread the net, approach; otherwise the cat might prove dangerous to him; if the cat, when freed, saw the Caṇḍāla drawing near he would immediately mount the tree and not waste his time in jumping on the mouse; Palita then could safely enter his hole 12. 136. 83-93; when the cat persisted in asking Palita to make haste, Palita replied as follows: “I have made treaty with one who is stronger than me, I have therefore to protect myself; no one has any regard for the doer of a good act, once the act has been fully done; hence all good acts must be done with a part left unfinished (न हि कश् चित् कृते कार्ये कर्तारं समवेक्षते । तस्मात् सर्वाणि कार्याणि सावशेषाणि कारयेत् 12. 136. 105); now only one cord remains; I shall cut down that too at proper time” 12. 136. 100-107; at dawn when the Caṇḍāla Parigha appeared, true to his word, Palita cut off the last cord; the freed cat, as expected by Palita, jumped up the tree and Palita entered the hole 12. 136. 109-116; when the Caṇḍāla left the scene, the cat asked Palita to come out of the hole and move freely among the cats without appre-hending any danger; he asked Palita to become his minister and even guide him like his father (अमात्यो मे भव प्राज्ञ पितेव हि प्रशाधि माम्) 12. 136. 119-126; but Palita refused to oblige; he told the cat that there were no natu-ral friends and no natural foes; hence there were no permanent friendships and no perma-nent enmities; friendships and enmities arise due to certain common or conflicting interests (नास्ति जात्या रीपुर् नाम मित्रं नाम न विद्यते । सामर्थ्ययोगाज् जायन्ते मित्राणि रिपवस् तथा ॥ नास्ति मैत्री स्थिरा नाम न च ध्रुवम् असौहृदम् । अर्थयुक्त्या हि जायन्ते मित्राणि रिपवस् तथा ॥ 12. 136. 132, 134); danger arising out of misplaced trust cuts at the very roots; the affection bet-ween them arose for some purpose; once that purpose was served, friendship lost its ground; mouse was food, and cat the eater; mouse was weak cat strong; there could be no real conciliation (सन्धि) among parties of uneven strength; Palita said he knew that it was the cat's food time; that was the reason why the cat was asking Palita to stir out; Palita finally told the cat that if he remembered Palita's good act let him wish well of the mouse (शिवं ध्यायस्व मे ऽत्रस्थः सुकृतं स्मर्यते यदि) 12. 136. 160-166; the cat made one more attempt to win the confidence of Palita and praised him 12. 136. 177-182; Palita did not relent; he recited two गाथास् of Uśanas (apparently 12. 136. 185-186) for the benefit of the cat the purport of which was that if one made conciliation (सन्धि) with a person stronger than himself to face a common enemy he should not repose trust in his partner after the purpose was served and that in all condi-tions one should protect one's life since wealth and children could be acquired if one remained alive; Palita concluded that the sum and substance of the नीतिशास्त्रस् was that distrust was the best policy (सङ्क्षेपो नीतिशास्त्राणाम् अविश्वासः परो मतः 12. 136. 187); Palita finally told the cat that the mouse must protect himself from the cat as the cat must protect himself from the Caṇḍāla; the cat, apparently scared at hearing the word ‘Caṇḍāla’, ran to his hole and Palita entered another hole; thus the intelligent Palita, all by himself, outwitted his many stronger enemies 12. 136. 182-192.
पाट: Pāṭa m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya described as ‘fast as wind’ (वातवेग) and ‘having excess of poison’ (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 16, 13, 1.
पाण्डर: Pāṇḍara m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Airāvata, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacri-fice of Janamejaya 1. 52. 10, 11, 1.
पात: Pāta m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Kauravya, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya 1. 52. 12, 11, 1.
पातर: Pātara m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Kauravya, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacri-fice of Janamejaya 1. 52. 12, 11, 1.
पारावत: Pārāvata m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Airāvata, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacri-fice of Janamejaya 1. 52. 10, 11, 1.
पारियात्र: Pāriyātra m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Airāvata, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacri-fice of Janamejaya 1. 52. 10. 11, 1.

Pāriyātra m.: Name of a mountain. A. Location: (1) Listed by Saṃjaya among the seven chief mountain ranges of the Bhāratavarṣa (सप्तैते कुलपर्वताः) 6. 10. 10. B. Importance: Listed by Brahman among the mountains who are called kings of mountains (एते पर्वत-राजानः) 14. 43. 4-5; (Are these mountains also to be looked upon as possessing the middle गुण, i. e. the quality of रजस् ? See Kāṣṭhavant). C. Past events: (1) Sage Gautama having reached the Pāriyātra moun-tain built his आश्रम there; he lived there for sixty thousand years 12. 127. 3-4; (2) A certain Dasyu, named Kāpavya, used to roam always on the ranges of the Pāriyātra (पारियात्रचरः सदा) 12. 133. 5; (3) One of the mountains seen by Mārkaṇḍeya in the belly of the Bāla (3. 186. 13 = Nārā-yaṇa 3. 187. 3) 3. 186. 104. D. Simile: Yudhiṣṭhira compared his four brothers, felled down by the Yakṣa, with the four moun-tains Himavant, Pāriyātra, Vindhya and Malaya 3. 297. 14.
पिङ्गल: Piṅgala m.: A mythical serpent. Son of Kadrū, listed among her sons by Sūta at the request of Śaunaka 1. 31. 9, 2.
पिङ्गलक: Piṅgalaka m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya; described as ‘fast as wind’ (वातवेग) and having excess of poison’ (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 14, 13, 1.
पिच्छिल: Picchila m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Vāsuki, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya; some snakes in this family were dark-red, others white, but all of them dreadful, huge in shape, and having excess of poison (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 5, 4.
पिञ्जरक: Piñjaraka m.: A mythical serpent, living in Bhogavatī Purī 5. 101. 11, 1. Son of Surasā and Kaśyapa 5. 101. 4, 17; description 5. 101. 5-7; also listed by Sūta among the sons of Kadrū 1. 31. 6, 2.
पिठरक: Piṭharaka m.: A mythical serpent. Son of Kadrū, listed among her sons by Sūta at the request of Śaunaka 1. 31. 14, 2. [See Pīṭharaka]
पिण्डभेत्तृ: Piṇḍabhettṛ m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Takṣaka, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya 1. 52. 7, 9, 1.
पिण्डार: Piṇḍāra m.: A mythical serpent, living in Bhogavatī Purī 5. 101. 14, 1. Son of Surasā and Kaśyapa 5. 101. 4, 17; description 5. 101. 5-7 [See Piṇḍāraka1]
पिण्डारक: Piṇḍāraka1 m.: A mythical serpent. Son of Kadrū, listed among her sons by Sūta at the request of Śaunaka 1. 31. 11, 2. [See Piṇḍāra]

Piṇḍāraka2 m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya; described as ‘fast as wind’ (वातवेग) and ‘having excess of poison’ (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 16, 13.

Piṇḍāraka nt.: Name of a तीर्थ। A. Location: In the Surāṣṭras (सुरा-ष्ट्रेषु) 3. 86. 16; in the Dvāravatī (ततो द्वारवतीं गच्छेत् … पिण्डारके नरः स्नात्वा) 3. 80. 82. B. Description: Auspicious (शुभ) and frequented by ascetics (तापसाचरित) 3. 86. 18. C. Special feature: At Piṇḍāraka there were seals (?) marked with lotuses which could be seen even in the days of the narrator of the Mahābhārata; this was its marvellous feature (तस्मिंस् तीर्थे महाभाग पद्म-लक्षणलक्षिताः । अद्यापि मुद्रा दृश्यन्ते तद् अद्भुतम् अरिन्दम ॥ ) 3. 80. 83; these lotuses (on the seals, or lotus flowers ?) bear the mark of trident (त्रिशूलाङ्कानि पद्-मानि दृश्यन्ते कुरुनन्दन) 3. 80. 84. D. Holiness: (1) Mahādeva is present there 3. 80. 84; (2) By bathing there one who is controlled and takes limited food (नियतो नियताशनः) obtains much gold (लभेद् बहु सुवर्णकम्) 3. 80. 82; (3) By bathing there and by staying there over-night (एकरात्रोषितो नरः) one gets the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma and is pure the next morning (प्रभातां शर्वरीं शुचिः) 13. 26. 54.
पिशङ्ग: Piśaṅga m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya; described as ‘fast as wind’ (वातवेग), ‘having excess of poison’ (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 15, 13.
पीठरक: Pīṭharaka m.: A mythical serpent, living in Bhogavatī Purī 5. 101. 14, 1. Son of Surasā and Kaśyapa 5. 101. 4, 17; description 5. 101. 5-7. [See Piṭharaka]
पुच्छण्डक: Pucchaṇḍaka m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Takṣaka, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacri-fice of Janamejaya 1. 52. 7, 9, 1.
पुण्डरीक: Puṇḍarīka m.: A mythical serpent, living in Bhogavatī Purī 5. 101. 13, 1. Son of Surasā and Kaśyapa 5. 101. 4, 17; description 5. 101. 5-7; one of those who received the white snake issuing from the mouth of Balarāma and entering the ocean 16. 5. 14, 12.
Puṇḍarīka nt.: Name of a तीर्थ। By bathing at this तीर्थ on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of a month (शुक्ल-पक्षे दशम्यां तु) one gets the fruit of a Puṇḍarīka sacrifice 3. 81. 69.
पुष्कर: Puṣkara m.: A mythical serpent. Son of Kadrū, listed among her sons by Sūta at the request of Śaunaka 1. 31. 13, 2.

Puṣkara1 nt., sg. and pl. (Puṣkarāṇi, Puṣkareṣu): Name of a तीर्थ; also called once Pitāmahasaras (3. 87. 13). A. Location: In the west 3. 87. 1. B. Description: Holy (पुण्य) 3. 87. 13; (पुण्यम् अन्तरिक्षे च पुष्करम्) 3. 81. 173; the lake of Pitāmaha Brahmadeva (पितामह-सरस्) 3. 87. 13; of the high-souled (Pitā-maha ?) (तीर्थे महात्मनः) 3. 80. 51; the तीर्थ of the god of gods (Brahmadeva) (देवदेवस्य तीर्थम्) 3. 80. 41; famous, famous in the three worlds (विख्यात, त्रै-लोक्यविश्रुत) 3. 80. 41. C. Epic events: (1) Arjuna, after his marriage with Subhadrā, spent with her at the Puṣkaras (पुष्करेषु) the remaining period of his exile 1. 213. 13; (2) Lomaśa advised Yudhiṣṭhira to bathe (जलं स्पृश) in all the Puṣkaras (पुष्क-रेषु … सर्वेषु) 3. 125. 12; (3) Pulastya recommended it to Bhīṣma 3. 80. 41. D. Past events: (1) Arjuna, while recounting the past austerities performed by Kṛṣṇa, said that formerly he once lived at the Puṣkaras (पुष्करेषु) for ten thousand and ten hundred years living only on water 3. 13. 1; (2) When the Pitāmaha was once engaged in a sacrifice at the Puṣkara (पुष्करस्थे पितामहे), the sages said that the sacrifice will not yield great fruit (नायं यज्ञो महाफलः) as the Sarasvatī was not to be seen there; hearing that, the Pitāmaha thought of the river and invited her to appear at the Puṣkaras (पुष्करेषु) which she did as the river Suprabhā; thus the Sarasvatī became manifest at the Puṣkaras (पुष्करेषु) for the sake of the Pitāmaha and for the satisfaction of the wise 9. 37. 11, 12, 14. E. Holiness: (1) There are आश्रमस् of the Vaikhānasas, the Siddhas, and the sages at the Puṣkara 3. 87. 13; one should settle down there (समाविशेत्) 3. 80. 41; gods and sages achieved there (पुष्क-रेषु) great perfection and were endowed with great merit (सिद्धिं समभिसंप्राप्ताः पुण्येन महतान्विताः) 3. 80. 47; (2) Prajāpati sang a गाथा at the Puṣkaras (पुष्करेषु) in praise of the Puṣkaras: If a spirited person (मनस्विन्) even mentally longs for the Puṣkaras (पुष्कराणि) his sins are destroyed and he is delighted in heaven (नाकपृष्ठे च मोदते) 3. 87. 14-15; (3) The wise say that one who is engaged in the worship of the manes and gods (पितृदेवा-र्चने रतः) and who takes bath (अभि-षेक) in this तीर्थ gets the fruit of a horse sacrifice ten times (अश्वमेधं दशगुणं प्रवदन्ति मनीषिणः); if a person of any one of the four classes bathes there these high-souled persons are then not born in a lower species (न वियोनिं व्रजन्त्य् एते स्नातास् तीर्थे महात्मनः); if one visits the Puṣkara especially on the full moon day of the month of Kārtika his fruit increases without ever being destroyed (फलं तत्राक्षयं तस्य वर्धते) 3. 80. 48, 51-52; stay at the Puṣkara on the full moon night of the Kārtika (कार्तिकीं वा वसेद् एकाम्) is equal to performing an Agnihotra for a full hundred years (वर्षशतं पूर्णं अग्निहोत्रम्) 3. 80. 57; (4) One who remembers the Puṣkara morning and evening with folded hands will have bathed in all the तीर्थस् and will get imperishable worlds in the abode of Brahman (उपस्पृष्टं भवेत् तेन सर्वती-र्थेषु भारत प्राप्नुयाच् च नरो लोकान् ब्रह्मणः सदने ऽक्षयान्) 3. 80. 53 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 3. 82. 33: उपस्पृष्टं स्नातं भवेत्); whatever sin is com-mitted by a man or a woman it gets destroyed as soon as one bathes in the Puṣkara (पुष्करे स्नातमात्रस्य) 3. 80. 54; if a wise person even mentally longs for the Puṣkaras (मनसाप्य् अभिकामस्य पुष्कराणि मनस्विनः) all his sins are cleansed and he is worshipped in heaven (नाकपृष्ठे च पूज्यते) 3. 80. 45; (5) At the Puṣkara ten thousand crores of तीर्थस् are present at all the three divisions of the day (सांनिध्यं पुष्करे येषां त्रिसन्-ध्यम्) 3. 83. 42; (6) At this तीर्थ the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, the Gandharvas, and the Apsa-rases are present at all times; Pitāmaha lived there happily for ever 3. 80. 43, 46; (7) The gods, the Daityas, and the Brahmani-cal sages practised austerities and, by the great religious merit thus acquired, they at-tained divine योग (दिव्ययोगाः), i. e., they attained perfection (सिद्धिं समभिसं-प्राप्ताः) 3. 80. 44, 47; (8) By living at the Puṣkara for twelve years a person who is controlled and pure (नियतः शुचिः) obtains the fruit of all sacrifices and goes to the world of Brahman 3. 80. 56; (9) Puṣkara is one of those place by visiting which one becomes auspicious, has a divine form, puts on heavenly garlands and being rich in heavenly fragrance delights in the world of the cows (? मोदन्ति गवां विमाने) 13. 105. 44, 48 (for citation see Karatoyinī); (10) Aṅgiras told Gautama that by bathing (विगाह्य) in the Puṣkara one rides in the Vimāna (विमानस्थः) and is awakened by the praises of the Apsarases 13. 26. 9; (11) Śaunaka advised Janamejaya to visit the Puṣkara; such visit gave the person longevity again in this life (लब्धायुर् जीविते पुनः) 12. 148. 11; (12) Parāśara told Janaka that more than bathing in the water of Puṣkara one should practise (lit. bathe in) austerities at the Puṣkaras (पुष्करेषु) and other holy places (अद्भ्यो भूयः प्लाव्यं तपसा वै शरीरम्) 12. 286. 37; (13) Puṣkara considered as the holy place of the mid-region (पृथिव्यां नैमिषम् पुण्यम् अन्तरिक्षे च पुष्करम्) 3. 81. 173; (however, Nī. on Bom. Ed. 3. 83. 202: अन्तरिक्षे सूर्य-चन्द्रादिमार्गे नक्षत्रादिचक्रे पुष्करं प्रापयतीत्य् अर्थः); (also see the section G. Importance and H. Simile below and section C. Epic events (2) and (3) above); F. Limitations: (i) Giving gifts of horses in very large numbers and of thousands of cows to the Brāhmaṇas at the Puṣkara (पुष्करेषु) was highly meritorious no doubt; (दशायुतानि चाश्वानाम् अयुतानि च विंशतिम् । पुष्करेषु द्विजातिभ्यः प्रादां गाश् च सहस्रशः); but that was not enough to enable one to reach the Brahma-loka—this is what Bhagīratha told Brahman 13. 106. 11; (ii) Sprinkling one's body with the water of the Puṣkara is not necessary for one who listens to the Bhārata (यो भारतं समधिगच्छति वाच्यमानं किं तस्य पुष्करजलैर् अभिषेचनेन) 1. 2. 242 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 1. 2. 392: पुषकरं आदि-तीर्थं शुण्डाग्रं वा तदुपाहृतजलैः); G. Importance: (1) Puṣkara is the first among the तीर्थस् as Madhusūdana is among all gods (यथा सुराणाम् सर्वेषाम् आदिस् तु मधुसूदनः । तथैव पुष्करं राजंस् तीर्थानाम् आदिर् उच्यते) 3. 80. 55; (2) It is not easy to go to the Puṣkara, not easy to perform austerities there or to give gifts there; to be able to live there is extremely difficult (दुष्करं पुष्करं गन्तुं दुष्-करं पुष्करे तपः । दुष्करं पुष्करे दानं वस्तुं चैव सुदुष्करम् ॥ ) 3. 80. 58; (3) Finds mention in the Daivata-Ṛṣi-Vaṃśa 13. 151. 14, 2. H. Simile: The entrance of the Kurukṣetra is as holy as the Puṣkaras (कुरुक्षेत्रस्य तद् द्वारम्  … संमिते पुष्कराणां च) 3. 81. 20-21. [See Pitāmahasaras]

Puṣkara2 m.: Name of a mountain in the Puṣkaradvīpa. In the Puṣkaradvīpa 6. 13. 24; described as full of precious stones and jewels (मणि-रत्नमन्त्) 6. 13. 24; god Prajāpati himself always lives there; all gods, along with the great sages, always wait on him worshipping it with agreeable words (तं पर्युपासते नित्यं … वाग्भिर् मनोनुकूलाभिः पूज-यन्तः) 6. 13. 24-25.

Puṣkara m.: Name of a द्वीप। A. Location: It is one of the seven द्वीपस् which are to the north of Jambū-dvīpa (उत्तरेषु तु … द्वीपेषु) 6. 13. 1; (सप्त त्व् अहं प्रवक्ष्यामि) 6. 12. 4. B. Characteristics: It has a mountain called Puṣkara which is full of jewels (पुष्करे पुष्करो नाम पर्वतो मणिरत्नमान्) 6. 13. 24; God Prajāpati lives on this mountain and is worshipped with agreeable words by gods and all great sages 6. 13. 24-25; for characteristics which are common to all Dvīpas see Kuśadvīpa.
पुष्प: Puṣpa m.: A mythical serpent, living in Bhogavatī Purī 5. 101. 13, 1. Son of Surasā and Kaśyapa 5. 101. 4, 17; description 5. 101. 5-7.
पुष्पदंष्ट्र: Puṣpadaṃṣṭra m.: A mythical serpent. Son of Kadrū, listed among her sons by Sūta at the request of Śaunaka 1. 31. 12, 2.
पूजनी: Pūjanī f.: A female bird (शकुनी 12. 137. 5; शकुनिका 12. 137. 108). A. Residence: She lived for a long time in the inner apartments (अन्तःपुर-वासिनी) of king Brahmadatta Kāmpilya 12. 137. 5. B. Qualities: Although born in the lower species she knew everything; she was conversant with धर्म and, like a जीव-जीवक (a bird who helps telling future ?; one who prophesies with the help of such a bird ? Nīla जीवजीवकः शाकुनिकः स हि अयं पक्षी अस्यां दिशि लाभं अस्याम् अलाभं दिशतीति वर्णयति । पक्षिविशेस इत्य् अन्ये on 12. 139. 6 Bom. Ed.), understood the meaning of the cries of all beings (रुतज्ञा सर्वभूतानां यथा वै जीवजीव-कः) 12. 137. 6. C. Her son's death: Her lustrous son grew in the palace with the king's son. Pūjanī used to get from the seashore two fruits, one for her son and one for the prince; one day the prince, while play-ing with the young bird, killed him in a secluded place; when Pūjanī returned with two fruits she found her young one dead; she lamented over her son's loss and blamed the Kṣatriyas who deserved no trust; she decided to take revenge and pierced the eyes of the prince with her talons; she said that a sinful act, deliberately committed, returned quickly on the doer and that taking revenge did not destroy one's good and bad (?) acts (इच्छ-यैव कृतं पापं सद्य एवोपसर्पति । कृतप्रतिक्रियं तेषां न नश्यति शुभा-शुभम्) 12. 137. 7-19. D. King Brahma-datta's dialogue with Pūjanī: Brahmadatta asked Pūjanī to continue to live with him since she had already retaliated for the misdeed of the prince; Pūjanī did not agree with the king saying that wise men recom-mended abandoning the place where misdeed was committed; enmities, once arisen, never subsided, hence no trust should be reposed in the enemy; the purpose for which she lived in the palace was no longer there; spirited men should abandon the place where after receiving honour they are dis-honoured; she said to the king: “I have lived here long enough; now I go, may you be happy” 12. 137. 21-30; the king pleaded with her saying that when some one retali-ated nothing wrong was committed and there-fore Pūjanī should stay on; Pūjanī did not consent saying that enmities never passed off (नास्ति वैरम् उपक्रान्तम् 12. 137. 34); no one should feel secure with the thought that reconciliation had come about; she pointed out to the king five causes of enmity: women, (ownership of) house, (bad) speech, rivalry, and misdeed (स्त्रीकृतं वास्तुजं वाग्जं ससपत्नापराधजम् 12. 137. 38); she lived with the king as long as nothing wrong happened; once that happened, she could trust the king no more; the king then put the entire responsibility of what had happened on Time (Kāla); since men were driven to act by Time nobody did anything wrong to any one; he had forgiven Pūjanī for her act, so should she forgive him for what (the prince) had done; Pūjanī retorted saying that if Kāla was to be blamed for everything, why did men seek to take revenge ? Why did Gods and Asuras fight with each other ? Why did men give and take medicines during illness ? She injured the king's son who had killed her son; now it was the king's turn to capture her; men wanted birds either for eating or for sporting; there was no third ground for the two to come together; if Pūjanī were to stay their enmity would be revived every time she remembered her son; she then recited two गाथास् which Uśanas had recited for Prahrāda (12. 137. 67-68); the purport of the गाथास् was that one who trusted the words of enemies was killed like a honey (-seeker ?) who was killed in a well) covered with dry grass (ते श्रद्दधाना वध्यन्ते मधु शुष्कतृणैर् यथा । Nī. शत्रुणा दर्शितं पुरःस्थितं मधु श्रद्दधाना शुष्कतृणैश् छन्ने प्रपाते यथा पतन्ति तद्वद् एते इत्य् अर्थः on 12. 139. 71 Bom. Ed.); enmities conti-nued because they were told to successive generations; when Brahmadatta further argued that trust had to be placed some-where to achieve one's objective or else one would live like a dead person, Pūjanī replied that if a person continued to run with injured feet, his feet got more hurt; she gave the king a long lecture on how one should guard one's interest by remaining alert and with constant exertion; one should leave the place where one was dishonoured; since Brahmadatta's son had done something which could not be repaired she had to leave the place; she also lectured on the king's duties (offering protection to subjects and not torturing them by levying heavy taxes); having said all that Pūjanī left (12. 137. 70-108); this conversation (सह भाषीतम्) between Brahmadatta and Pūjanī narrated by Bhīṣma to Yudhiṣṭhira (12. 137. 4-109).
पूर्ण: Pūrṇa m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Vāsuki, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacri-fice of Janamejaya; some of the serpents in this family were dark-red, some white; all were ferocious, huge, and having excess of poison (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 5, 4, 6.
पूर्णदंष्ट्र: Pūrṇadaṃṣṭra m.: A mythical serpent. Son of Kadrū, listed by Sūta among her sons at the request of Śaunaka 1. 31. 12, 2.
पूर्णमुख: Pūrṇamukha m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya; described as ‘fast as wind’ (वातवेग), ‘having excess of poison’ (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 14, 13, 1
पूर्णाङ्गद: Pūrṇāṅgada m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya; described as ‘fast as wind’ (वातवेग) and ‘having excess of poison’ (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 14, 13, 1.
पृथुश्रवस्: Pṛthuśravas m.: A mythical serpent. One of those who received the white snake issuing from the mouth of Balarāma and entering the ocean 16. 5. 14, 12.
पैल: Paila m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Vāsuki, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacr-fice of Janamejaya; some of the serpents in this family were dark-red, some white; all were ferocious, huge, and having excess of poison (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 5, 4, 6.
पोतक: Potaka m.: A mythical serpent, living in Bhogavatī Purī 5. 101. 11, 1. Son of Surasā and Kaśyapa 5. 101. 4, 17; description 5. 101. 5-7.
प्रकालन: Prakālana m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Vāsuki, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya; some of the serpents in this family were dark-red, others white; all were ferocious, huge, and having excess of poison (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 5, 4, 6.
प्रभाकर: Prabhākara m.: A mythical serpent. Son of Kadrū, listed among her sons by Sūta at the request of Śaunaka 1. 31. 15, 2.

Prabhākara nt. (sg.): Name of a Varṣa in the Kuśadvīpa. A. Location: To the north of Jambu-dvīpa (उत्तरेषु तु … द्वीपेषु) 6. 13. 1; it is the sixth Varṣa among of the seven Varṣas of Kuśadvīpa (षष्ठम् वर्षं प्रभाकरम् 6. 13. 13. B. Characteristic: Gods and Gandharvas sport there and are happy, men do not die; there are neither Dasyus nor Mleccha people on these Varṣas; all people are fair and very delicate 6. 13. 13-15 (for citation see Audbhida).
प्रमोद: Pramoda m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Airāvata, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacri-fice of Janamejaya 1. 52. 10, 1, 3.
प्ररुज: Praruja m.: A mythical bird. He fought with Garuḍa when the latter was on his expedition to fetch अमृत; Garuḍa killed Praruja inflicting wounds on him with wings, nails and beak 1. 28. 19, 20, 22. [Ac-cording to Nī., name of a Yakṣa, cf. अश्व-क्रन्दादयो नव यक्षाः on 1. 32. 18 Bom. Ed.].
प्रलिह: Praliha m.: A mythical bird. He fought with Garuḍa when the latter was on his expedition to fetch अमृत; Garuḍa killed Praliha inflicting wounds on him with wings, nails and beak 1. 28. 19, 20, 22. [According to Nī., name of a Yakṣa, cf. अश्वक्रन्दादयो नव यक्षाः on 1. 32. 18 Bom. Ed.].
प्रवेपन: Pravepana m.: A mythical serpent. Born in the कुल of Takṣaka, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacri-fice of Janamejaya 1. 52. 8, 7, 9.
प्रहस: Prahasa m.: A mythical serpent, Born in the कुल of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, listed by Sūta among those offered in the snake sacrifice of Janamejaya; described as ‘fast as wind’ (वातवेग), and ‘having excess of poison’ (विषोल्बण) 1. 52. 14, 13, 1.
प्रह्लाद: Prahlāda m.: A mythical serpent. One of the serpents who, without feeling fatigue (विगतक्लम), wait upon Varuṇa in his सभा; described as marked with banner (पताकिन्), round spots (मण्डलिन्), and hooded (फणवन्त्) 2. 9. 10. 11.
प्राकारकर्ण: Prākārakarṇa m.: An owl, living on the mountain Himavant 3. 191. 4. Sage Mārkaṇḍeya and king (राजर्षि) Indradyumna approached the owl Prākāra-karṇa since he was guessed by Mārkaṇḍeya to be older than both of them; king Indradyumna asked Prākārakarṇa if he recognized the king; Prākārakarṇa thought for a while and said he did not; when asked by Indradyumna if Prākārakarṇa knew any one older than he, the owl directed the king to the crane Nāḍījaṅgha living in the lake Indradyumna; then the king Indradyumna took both Mārkaṇḍeya and Prākārakarṇa to Nāḍījaṅgha 3. 191. 5-10.
परशु: Paraśu m.: An axe (not named) used as a weapon by Rāma Jāmadagnya. Described as having a sharp and shining edge (तीक्ष्णधार 13. 14. 137, दीप्तधार 13. 14. 139), of extremely fearful front (सुरौद्रास्य 13. 14. 139), it shines like a burning flame of fire (दीप्तवह्निशिखो-पम 13. 14. 139); since it belongs to Śiva, it is circled by the neck of the ser-pent (सर्पकण्ठाग्रवेष्टित) 13. 14. 139; it was given by Śiva to Rāma Jāmadagnya when he was satisfied with Rāma 13. 14. 137; Rāma used it to cut off the head of his mother Reṇukā at the instance of his father Jamadagni 3. 116. 14; Rāma used it also to kill in battle the universal ruler Kārtavīrya 13. 14. 137; he used this weapon (शस्त्र) to kill the sons of Kārtavīrya and the Kṣatriyas who were his followers 3. 117. 7-8; Rāma exterminated the Kṣatriyas from this earth twenty-one times using this axe 13. 14. 138; (3. 117. 9).
परानीकभिद्: Parānīkabhid m.: Name (?) of a particular arrangement of the army (व्यूह). The Pāṇḍava army was arranged this way on the seventeenth day of the battle; it is described as ‘having no parallel’ (अप्र-तिम) 8. 31. 1; it was arranged by Arjuna 8. 32. 3; apparently Dhṛṣṭadyumna, guarded on two sides by the sons of Draupadī, stood at its head 8. 32. 4, 6; but at the start of the war Arjuna rushed to the front 8. 31. 36; 8. 32. 7; it was used against the Kaurava army which was arranged accord-ing to the Bārhaspatya vyūha 8. 31. 26.
परिघ: Parigha m.: A club (not named) mentioned as a weapon of Aryaman. He roamed around with it when he got ready to help Indra in his fight with Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna at the time of the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest 1. 218. 34.
परिवृत्त: Parivṛtta nt.: One of the twenty-one movements (सो ऽचरद् विविधान् मार्गान् प्रकारान् एकविंशतिम्) used while fighting with a sword and a shield. Dhṛṣṭadyumna used it when he, with a sword and a shield in hand, wanted to attack Droṇa who was shooting arrows at him 7. 164. 145-148.
पर्जन्यास्त्र: Parjanyāstra, Pārjaynāstra nt.: Name of a missile used to produce clouds or water. Arjuna created clouds by releasing it (पार्जन्येनासृजद् घनान्) when he display-ed his skill in the use of missiles to all those assembled in the arena 1. 125. 19; Arjuna employed it by reciting मन्त्रस् on the shining arrow with which he pierced the earth to produce jets of water for Bhīṣma (संधाय च शरं दीप्तम् अभिमन्त्र्य महायशाः । पर्जन्यास्त्रेण संयोज्य … अविध्यत् पृथिवीं पार्थः) 6. 116. 22-23. [Parjanyāstra apparently different from Vāruṇāstra for which see below].
पर्वत: Parvata m.: Mountain (not named), used as a weapon by Tvaṣṭṛ. Tvaṣṭṛ held it when he got ready to help Indra in his fight with Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna at the time of burning the Khāṇḍava forest 1. 218. 33; a heavenly weapon (not named) of Tvaṣṭṛ, known to Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa, is referred to by Bhīṣma 6. 116. 38-39. [Identical with Pārvata ?]
पाञ्चजन्य: Pāñcajanya m.: Name of the conch of Kṛṣṇa. A. Origin: Ocean (समुद्र 1. 19. 3) said to be the origin of Pāñcajanya (पाञ्च-जन्यस्य जननम्) 1. 19. 10. B. History: It belonged to the demon (?) Pañcajana residing in Pātāla; after conquering Varuṇa in the waters of the ocean, Kṛṣṇa killed Pañcajana and obtained the conch from him 7. 10. 19-20. C. Description: water-born (जलज) 3. 15. 20; 3. 21. 30; (अम्बुज) 7. 78. 35; (सलिलज) 7. 102. 59; heavenly (दिव्य) 5. 47. 58; 6. 1. 17; 6. 23. 14; 7. 10. 20; king of conches or excellent among conches (शङ्खराज्) 7. 85. 36, 38; 7. 102. 59; (शङ्खवर) 6. 47. 24; 8. 68. 56; (शङ्ख-प्रवर) 3. 21. 12; 7. 64. 20; (सर्व-शङ्खवर) 7. 79. 11; white in colour (हिमावदात) 8. 68. 56; (गोक्षीर-कुन्देन्दुमृणालरजतप्रभ) 3. 21. 30; adorned with gold and jewels (हेमरत्न-परिष्कृत) 6. 47. 24, and covered with golden net (सुवर्णजालावतत) 8. 68. 56; produc-ing loud sound (सुघोष) 8. 68. 55; (महा-स्वन) 8. 68. 56. D. Sound: Its sound (नाद, निर्घोष, रव, निनद) was frightful (भैरव) 7. 56. 36; (घोर) 7. 102. 57, 58; the sound (निर्घोष) was produced only on the ऋषभ note (आर्षभेणैव पूरि-तम्) 7. 56. 36 [Nī. आर्षभेण ऋष्भस्वर-प्रकारेण on 7. 79. 39 Bom. Ed.]; Kṛṣṇa filled it fully with breath while blowing it (3. 21. 30) and the sound caused the whole world, including the पाताल, the heaven, and the guar-dians of the quarters, to tremble 7. 51. 42; Kṛṣṇa blew it forcefully to produce a shrill note (पाञ्चजन्यं च बलवद् दध्मौ तारेण केशवः) 7. 78. 37; the sound excelled all other sounds and filled the heaven and the earth 7. 79. 13; 7. 102. 59; 8. 37. 19; 8. 68. 57; it reverberated in forests, mountains, rivers and directions 8. 68. 57; 6. 55. 102; it produced sound like the one heard at the flash of a lightning 5. 149. 65. E. Effect of the sound: The sound caused delight to warriors on Kṛṣṇa's side 5. 149. 65; 6. 1. 17; but the enemies felt dejected (5. 47. 59; 8. 37. 20), and trembled; they lost courage, and the draught-animals passed urine and dung 7. 64. 21-24; 6. 1. 18; 6. 67. 2; 7. 3. 19; 8. 68. 55; 9. 3. 19; hearing it enemies, strong and weak, fell on the ground 7. 78. 38. F. Uses: (1) In the epic war: (i) when the Pāṇḍava warriors reached Kurukṣetra they blew their respective conches and so did Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna 5. 149. 64-65; (ii) when the two armies were arrayed against each other, ready to fight, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna blew their conches 6. 1. 17; 6. 23. 15; (iii) Kṛṣṇa blew his Pāñcajanya at the start of the second day's war 6. 47. 25 (and presumably at the start of the war on all subsequent days); (iv) when Arjuna vowed to fight more seriously with Bhīṣma 6. 55. 102; (v) when Arjuna rushed at Bhīṣma who was fighting with other Pāṇḍavas 6. 67. 2; (vi) Kṛṣṇa blew his conch when Arjuna took the vow to kill Jayadratha 7. 51. 41; (vii) at the start of the day on which Jaya-dratha was killed 7. 64. 20; when Arjuna was heading forward looking for Jayadratha in the Kaurava army 7. 75. 31; as Arjuna was nearing Jayadratha 7. 78. 37; 7. 79. 11; at the end of the day when Jayadratha was killed 7. 123. 41; [It is significant that the sounding of Pāñcajanya is mentioned on many occa-sions on the day on which Arjuna had to fulfil his difficult vow to kill Jayadratha]; (viii) Kṛṣṇa blew it when Arjuna got rid of the Saṃśaptakas who had overwhelmed both of them 8. 37. 19, 15-17; (ix) at the death of Karṇa and the subsequent rout of the Kaurava army 8. 68. 57; (x) at the fall of Duryodhana 9. 60. 65; (2) Outside the epic war: Kṛṣṇa blew it to challenge Śālva when he reached Śālva's Saubhapura 3. 15. 20; when Kṛṣṇa started fighting with Śālva 3. 21. 12; when, during his fight with Śālva, Kṛṣṇa killed many Dānavas 3. 21. 29-30; G. Its use as a signal: (1) Kṛṣṇa had told Dāruka, his charioteer, that when he heard the sound of Pāñcajanya he was to rush to the battle-field driving Kṛṣṇa's chariot for its eventual use by Kṛṣṇa to enable Arjuna to fulfil his vow to kill Jayadratha 7. 56. 36; (2) The sound was once interpreted by Droṇa to mean that Arjuna wanted to set aside other heroes and attack Bhīṣma 6. 108. 14; (3) It was once interpreted by Yudhiṣṭhira to mean that Arjuna was in danger 7. 85. 35; on another occasion, the sound meant for Yudhiṣṭhira the death of Arjuna, and hence Kṛṣṇa's starting to fight 7. 102. 32-33. H. End: When the time of the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis and the Andhakas arrived the blowing of Pāñca-janya in their houses was accompanied by the harsh braying of the asses 16. 3. 15 [नदन्तं पाञ्चजन्यं च वृष्ण्यन्धक-निवेशने । समन्तात् प्रत्यवाश्यन्त रासभा दारुणस्वराः ॥ Does Pāñcajanya here refer not to Kṛṣṇa's special conch, but to the conches in general in the houses of the Vṛṣṇis and the Andhakas ?].
पारमेष्ठ्य: Pārameṣṭhya (astra) nt.: Name of a missile of Prajāpati. According to Bhīṣma it was known to Arjuna and perhaps to Kṛṣṇa 6. 116. 38-39. [See Brahmāstra]
पार्जन्य: Pārjanya (astra) nt.: Name of a missile 1. 125. 19 [See Parjanyāstra]
पार्वत: Pārvata (astra) nt.: Name of a missile. When Arjuna displayed his skill in the use of missiles, he released mountains by the employment of the Pārvata astra (पार्व-तेनासृजद् गिरीन्) 1. 125. 20. [See Parvata]
पाश: Pāśa m. (pl.): Noose used as a missile (पाश generally used in pl., but also rarely in sg. 1. 218. 31). A. Association with Varuṇa: Listed as a missile of Ambupa (Varuṇa) 8. 66. 15; hence called वारुण अस्त्र 4. 56. 14; Varuṇa has epithets like पाशभृत् 6. 46. 7; 6. 103. 17; पाशवन्त् 7. 64. 15; पाशिन् 8. 29. 28. B. Description: Described as heavenly (दिव्य) 3. 42. 31; 3. 89. 12; 12. 5. 13-14; fierce (घोर) 3. 190. 60; 7. 53. 43; irresi-stible (अनिवारण) 3. 42. 27. C. Use made by Varuṇa: (1) In battles: Varuṇa bound thousands of Daityas with them in the fight with Tārakāsura 3. 42. 28; during Varuṇa's fight with the demons, Bali, son of Virocana, was bound by the पाशस् 12. 220. 18; Bali would be free from these पाशस् at the turn of time (मोक्षयन्ते वारुणाः पाशास् तवेमे कालपर्ययात्) 12. 220. 110; at a time only one पाश of Bali will be released (एकैकस् ते तदा पाशः क्रमशः प्रतिमोक्ष्यते) 12. 220. 114; Varuṇa equi-pped himself with पाश (sg.) when he got ready to help Indra in his fight with Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna at the Khāṇḍava forest 1. 218. 31; (2) To punish the sinners: Varuṇa has one thousand पाशस् with which he binds a liar; when the liar is to be released he is freed of one पाश at the end of each year 2. 61. 67-68; sinners in general bound by the पाशस् of Varuṇa 12. 96. 20; 3. 190. 60; one who does not give what he has promised to give, or one who takes back what has been given, is bound by the पाशस् of Varuṇa 13. 61. 72; every one is afraid at the sight of Varuṇa's पाशस् 12. 220. 89; Varuṇa binding with पाशस् referred to as संयम (?) (वारुणे चैव संयमे) 2. 69. 16 (Nī. संयमे वशीकरणे on Bom. Ed. 2. 78. 19]. D. Pāśas obtained by Arjuna: Arjuna received from Varuṇa the पाशस् along with the secret of withdrawing them (प्रतिगृह्-णीष्व कौन्तेय सरहस्यनिवर्तनान्); if Arjuna used them on his stretched bow, even Antaka could not get rid of them; with their use Arjuna could destroy every Kṣatriya on the earth 3. 42. 27, 29, 30; Arjuna's receiv-ing the अस्त्र of Varuṇa, without naming it, referred to 3. 89. 12; 3. 164. 29; 4. 56. 14; 7. 53. 43; 12. 5. 13-14. [See Vāruṇa1, Vāruṇa2]
पाशुपत: Pāśupata nt., (m.): Name of the missile of Śiva 7. 57. 16. A. Description: Heavenly (दिव्य) 3. 41. 7; 3. 163. 51; 7. 41. 7; 7. 57. 62; 13. 14. 124; large, of huge shape (महत्) 3. 41. 13; 13. 14. 124; (महाकाय) 13. 14. 125; (महास्त्र) 1. 1. 109; 8. 57. 44; (पर-मास्त्र) 7. 57. 16; fierce (घोर) 3. 41. 7, 22; 5. 47. 100; 7. 57. 79; (सुघोर) 8. 57. 44; (महाघोर) 13. 14. 124; (रौद्र) 3. 163. 48; eternal (सनातन) 3. 163. 49; burning (जाज्वलत्) 3. 41. 22; (सस्फुलिङ्गं … विसृजन्तम् (mas.) इवान-लम्) 13. 14. 125; (उद्गिरन्तम् (mas.) इवानलम्) 13. 14. 126; itself irresistible (अप्रतिहत) 3. 163. 51; (दूरासद) 3. 163. 52, but resisting all other missiles (सर्वा-स्त्रप्रतिषेधन) 3. 163. 51; (सर्वशस्त्र-विघातन) 13. 14. 127; unsurpassed, in-describable (अद्वितीयम् अनिर्देश्यम्) 13. 14. 125; frightful to all beings (सर्वभूत-भयावह) 13. 14. 125; difficult to be endured even by gods, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas (दुष्प्रसहं सुरदानवराक्षसैः) 3. 163. 52; destroying the enemies and their armies (उत्सादनम् अमित्राणां परसेनानिकर्त-नम्) 3. 163. 52; capable of destroying the three worlds (त्रैलोक्यसंहारकर) 8. 57. 44; described as having a terrible bodily form —having one foot, large teeth, a thousand heads and bellies, and a thousand arms, tongues, and eyes—(एकपादं महादं-ष्ट्रं सहस्रशिरसोदरम् । सहस्रभुज-जिह्वाक्षम्) 13. 14. 126. B. Use by Śiva: (1) Śiva killed with it all Daityas in the battle 7. 57. 16; (all the enemies of gods) 7. 57. 65; (2) Śiva charged his arrow with the Pāśupata missile and shot it to burn the त्रिपुरस् of the three sons of Tāraka Asura 8. 24. 115, 120; (8. 24. 4, 10-12); 13. 14. 128. C. Śiva gave it to (1) Arjuna: Two accounts: (i) Arjuna desired to have Śiva's Pāśupata missile so that he could burn the Dānavas, the Rākṣasas, the Bhūtas, the Piśācas, the Gandharvas and the mythical serpents (पन्नगस्) in battle; he could then be a match for Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, and Karṇa 3. 41. 7, 9, 11; Arjuna called it Brahma-śiras which was terrific and of fierce power (यत् तद् ब्रह्मशिरो नाम रौद्रं भीम-पराक्रमम्) 3. 41. 8; Śiva ready to give Pāśupata, his dear weapon (दयितम् अस्त्रम्), to Arjuna as he was capable of possessing (धारण), releasing (मोक्ष), and with-drawing (संहार) it 3. 41. 13; to receive it, Arjuna purified himself and remained fully attentive (शुचिर् भूत्वा समाहितः); he folded his hands and said to Śiva ‘recite (the mantra)’ (अधीष्व); Śiva then taught it to Arjuna together with its secrets and mode of withdrawal (सरहस्यनिवर्तनम्) 3. 41. 17-18; the missile, like the God of Death in bodily form, then waited on Arjuna; at that time the earth trembled and there was a loud sound of conches, drums and भेरिस् by thou-sands; the gods and demons saw the missile in bodily form standing near Arjuna 3. 41. 17-22; 1. 1. 109; 3. 163. 48, 51; 6. 116. 38; 8. 57. 44; (ii) During the night, after Arjuna took the vow to kill Jayadratha the next day before sunset, Kṛṣṇa advised Arjuna to acquire the knowledge of the great Pāśupata missile from Śiva in order to be able to accomplish his vow; Kṛṣṇa advised Arjuna to mentally approach god Śiva; Arjuna touched water (संस्पृश्याम्भः), sat down on the ground, and mentally went to Bhava (Śiva) 7. 57. 17-19; Arjuna praised Śiva and made him favourable to give the missile 7. 57. 59; Śiva told Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa that nearby there was a lake of nectar where he had left his divine bow and arrow; he asked them to get his bow and arrow 7. 57. 64-65; when they brought the bow and arrow, a Brahmacārin came from the side of Śiva; he held the bow and, putting the arrow on it, drew it according the prescriptions (व्यकर्षच् चापि विधिवत् सशरं धनुर् उत्तमम् 7. 57. 75); having seen how the Brahmacārin held the bow in his grip, how he drew the string, and the posture adopted by him (तस्य मौर्वीं च मुष्टिं च स्थानं चालक्ष्य पाण्डवः 7. 57. 76), and having heard the मन्त्र recited by Śiva, Arjuna understood the way how to employ Pāśupata; the arrow was shot by the Brahmacārin in the lake and the bow was again placed in it; Arjuna then remembered the boon Śiva granted to him during his stay in the forest (आरण्यक) and his meeting Śiva, and wished that he might now receive the boon; knowing Ariuna's mind, Śiva gave him the boon, the Pāśupata missile, and wished him success in accomplishing his vow; Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna bowed down to Śiva and, when permitted to leave, delighted they returned to their camp, 7. 57. 73-81; (Śiva gave missile to Arjuna 7. 173. 100); (2) Besides Arjuna, Kṛṣṇa knew the use of Pāśupata 7. 57. 79; 8. 57. 44; Bhīṣma is not so sure about Kṛṣṇa's knowledge of the Pāśupata 6. 116. 39. D. Effects: The missile, when released, produced thousands of tridents (शूलस्), fierce maces (गदाश् चोग्रप्रदर्शनाः), and charmed arrows having the form of serpents (शराश् चाशीविषाकाराः संभवन्त्य् अनुमन्त्रिताः) 3. 41. 10. E. Restrictions on its use: Arjuna was specifically told by Śiva that the missile was never to be used against men (न प्रयोज्यं भवेद् एतन् मानुषेषु कथंचन); Arjuna was to use the missile only if he was under severe pressure (पीड्यमानेन बलवत्), or if he wished to ward off the missiles used by his opponents (अस्त्राणां प्रति-घाते च सर्वथैव प्रयोजयेः) 3. 163. 49-50; 3. 41. 15; if used against ordinary persons it would burn the entire world 3. 41. 15. F. Use in the epic war: (1) Arjuna in his message to the Kauravas, sent through Saṃjaya, threatened that he would use the Pāśupata missile against them in the war 5. 47. 100; Kṛṣṇa told Karṇa that in the ‘sacrifice to be performed with the wea-pons’ (शस्त्रयज्ञ 5. 139. 29), the मन्त्रस् recited by Arjuna while releasing the Pāśupata and other missiles would serve as the मन्त्रस् used while performing a sacrifice 5. 139. 31; (2) Droṇa used Pāśupata against Arjuna and it was repelled (जघान) by Arjuna presumably by using the same missile 7. 163. 28; (3) Karṇa used it against Yudhi-ṣṭhira and hence Kṛṣṇa apprehended Yudhi-ṣṭhira's death in the war 8. 43. 21, 18. G. Status: The Pāśupata missile surpassed all other missiles like Brāhma, Nārāyaṇa, Aindra, Āgneya, and Vāruṇa; it could destroy all weapons (सर्वशस्त्रविघातन) 13. 14. 127; even gods like Indra, Yama, Kubera, Varuṇa, and Vāyu did not know it 3. 41. 14; there was none who could not be killed by it; besides its use on an arrow, it could be released even by mind, eye, and speech (मनसा चक्षुषा वाचा धनुषा च निपात्यते) 3. 41. 16.
पिनाक: Pināka1 nt.: Name of the bow of Śiva (of Rudra, who killed cattle with it 6. 58. 58; 6. 59. 16; 10. 3. 29). A. Association with Śiva: Śiva told Umā that he held Pināka to accomplish the objectives of the gods 13. 127. 48; 13. 128. 7; Upamanyu saw Śiva with his Pināka bow 13. 14. 122; considered as a special weapon of Hara (Śiva) 8. 66. 15; hence Śiva is called पिनाकिन् 1. 28. 20; 3. 39. 25; 3. 40. 31; 3. 42. 1, 3; 3. 104. 11; 3. 221. 18; 5. 168. 5; 6. 58. 52; 7. 69. 56; 7. 172. 59; 7. 173. 33; 8. 49. 93; 9. 43. 33; 12. 149. 110; 12. 278. 27; 13. 15. 11; पिनाकधृक् 3. 40. 27; 3. 93. 12; 3. 163. 5, 42; 4. 21. 59; 6. 58. 52; 7. 172. 73; 7. 173. 99; 12. 274. 31, 48; 13. 17. 72, 133; 13. 127. 50; 13. 132. 27; 13. 145. 10; 14. 77. 44; पिनाकपाणि 3. 40. 1; 8. 24. 102; 10. 3. 29 (Rudra); 13. 14. 151; 13. 128. 20; पिनाकहस्त 12. 320. 31. B. Origin: Śiva wanted to tame sage Uśanas, a Bhārgava-relative (भार्गवदायादो मुनिः 12. 278. 7) because Uśanas had taken away the riches of Kubera; so Śiva, with शूल in hand, went to Uśanas; Uśanas using his Yogic powers appeared on the tip of the शूल; Śiva then bent the शूल to get Uśanas into his hand; the शूल, bent by the hand (पाणि), was called by Śiva ‘पिनाक’ (आनतेनाथ शूलेन पाणिना-मिततेजसा । पिनाकम् इति चोवाच शूलम् उग्रायुधः प्रभुः 12. 278. 18-19; Nīla. uses this description to suggest a fanciful etymology of पिनाक: शूलम् एव पिनाक-पदेन उवाच । यतः पाणिना अनामयत् अतः पिनाकम् । तेन आद्यपदस्याद्यन्त-वर्णाभ्यां द्वितीयस्य मध्यमाभ्यां कप्रत्यययुक्ताभ्यां पिनाकपदम् निष्प-न्नम् इति योगप्रदर्शनं कृतम् Bom. Ed. 12. 289. 18). C. Description: Illustrious (श्रीमत्) 3. 40. 3 (not named); its splendour like that of a thousand lightnings (इन्द्रा-युधसहस्राभ 13. 14. 122). D. Com-parisons: (1) Bhīma's गदा compared with Pināka (of Rudra) 6. 58. 58; 6. 59. 16; or Bhīma with his गदा compared with Pinākin (Śiva) holding his Pināka 6. 58. 52; (2) Arjuna's Añjalika arrow with which he killed Karṇa compared with Pināka (i. e. the arrow shot from Pināka) 8. 67. 18; (3) The arrow of Karṇa with which he removed the किरीट of Arjuna supposed to have achieved something not possible for Hara's (Śiva's) Pināka (i. e. for the arrow shot from Pināka) 8. 66. 15. [See Pināka2]

Pināka2 m. (pl.): A kind of weapon (a शूल with a bend and hence looking like the staff of a strung bow ?) Ghaṭotkaca and Alāyudha fought each other using various weapons including Pinākas (ततो नानाप्रहरणैर् अन्योन्यम् अभिवर्ष-ताम् । आयसैः परिघैः … पिनाकैः … ) 7. 153. 21-22; the Rākṣasas of Ghaṭotkaca struck down the Kaurava warriors with various weapons including Pinākas ( … वज्रैः पिनाकैर् अशनिप्रहारैः) 7. 154. 36. [See Pināka1]
पैतामह: Paitāmaha adj.: of the missile of Pitāmaha. Arjuna was to learn it along with the other divine missiles at the residence of Indra in the heaven 3. 164. 30. [See Brahmāstra]
पैशाच: Paiśāca adj. (pl.): of व्यूह (arrange-ment of the army) known to the Piśācas. Every day Bhīṣma arranged the army of the Kauravas in different व्यूहस्, some of those being the Paiśācas (दिवसे दिवसे प्राप्ते भीष्मः शान्तनवो युधि । आसुरान् अकरोद् व्यूहान् पैशाचान् अथ राक्षसान्) 6. 104. 16.
पौण्ड्र: Pauṇḍra m.: Name of the conch of Bhīmasena. Large in size (महाशङ्ख), Bhīma blew it at the start of the battle on the first day 6. 23. 15; he blew it on the second day 6. 47. 25; (and presumably on every subse-quent day, as also on many other occasions during the war although not specifically named each time).
पौरन्दर: Paurandara adj.: of the missile of Purandara (Indra). Arjuna told Karṇa that he was well-versed in the use of this missile due to his teacher's instruction (निष्ठितो गुरुशासनात्) 1. 181. 20.
प्रज्ञास्त्र: Prajñāstra nt.: Name of a missile. Droṇa used Prajñāstra to bring the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra back to consciousness (अथ प्रत्यागतप्राणास् तव पुत्रा महारथाः 6. 73. 50), who had become unconscious due to the Pramohanāstra of Dhṛṣṭadyumna 6. 73. 42-43, 47, 49; Vibhīṣaṇa brought Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to consciousness (बोधयाम् आस तौ वीरौ; प्रबोधितौ; तौ लब्ध-संज्ञौ) who were bound by the arrows of Indrajit and who had apparently lost consciousness 3. 273. 5, 7; (both Droṇa and Vibhīṣaṇa recited only the मन्त्रस् of Prajñāstra without using them on the arrow ?).
प्रमोहनास्त्र: Pramohanāstra, Mohanāstra nt.: Name of a missile. Used by Dhṛṣṭadyumna to kill (जिघां-सुः) the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra who showered arrows on him; Dhṛṣṭadyumna employed Pramohanāstra on them due to which they lost consciousness 6. 73. 42, 43, 47; Droṇa removed the effect of the missile (Moha-nāstra) by using Prajñāstra 6. 73. 49.
प्रसृत: Prasṛta nt.: One of the twenty-one movements (सो ऽचरद् विविधान् मार्गान् प्रकारान् एकविंशतिम्) used while fighting with a sword and a shield. Dhṛṣṭadyumna used it when he, with a sword and a shield in his hand, wanted to attack Droṇa who shot arrows at him 7. 164. 145-148.
प्रस्वाप: Prasvāpa nt.: Name of a missile which sent the adversary to sleep. It was fashioned by Viśvakarman (विश्वकृतम्) and it belonged properly to Prajāpati (प्राजापत्यम्) 5. 184. 12; des-cribed as ‘dear’ (सुदयित, दयित) 5. 184. 11; 5. 184. 15; 5. 185. 23; it was known to Bhīṣma in his former life (पूर्वस्मिन् देहधारणे); in his long-drawn fight with Rāma Jāmadagnya, when Bhīṣma was deject-ed, the eight Vipras (Vasus) reminded him of this missile in a dream and told him that it would flash upon him again (इदम् अस्त्रम् सुदयितम् प्रत्यभिज्ञास्यते भ-वान्); the missile was not known to Rāma Jāmadagnya, and to no one else on the earth; the Vipras advised Bhīṣma to employ it forcefully (भृशं संयोजयस्व 5. 184. 13) against Rāma Jāmadagnya; as a result Rāma would not die but just go to sleep; in its use against his teacher Rāma, Bhīṣma would incur no sin; Bhīṣma will have thus defeated Rāma with Prasvāpāstra (to be awakened by him later by using Saṃbo-dhanāstra); since Rāma could not be killed in battle, he was to be defeated by using Prasvāpāstra; the Vipras told Bhīṣma that a hero sent to sleep in battle and the one killed were considered by them equal (प्रसुप्तं वा मृतं वापि तुल्यं मन्या-महे वयम् 5. 184. 16) 5. 184. 9-17; the next day when Bhīṣma thought of the missile for employing it, it flashed in his mind (चिन्तितं च तद् अस्त्रं मे मनसि प्रत्य-भात् तदा) 5. 185. 22-23; the gods, appear-ing in the heaven, however, forbade Bhīṣma from using Prasvāpa against Rāma; as Bhīṣma put the arrow on his bow, Nārada drew Bhīṣma's attention to what the gods asked him and he told Bhīṣma not to insult Rāma who was his teacher; the eight Vipras also asked Bhīṣma to do what Nārada told him, since therein lay the welfare of the worlds (एतद् धि परमं श्रेयो लोकानाम्); hence Bhīṣma withdrew the missile; when Rāma saw Bhīṣma withdrawing the missile he accepted defeat at the hands of Bhīṣma (दृष्ट्वा तद् अस्त्रं विनिवर्तितं वै । जितो ऽस्मि भीष्मेण सुमन्दबुद्धिर् इत्य् एव वाक्यं सहसा व्यमुञ्चत्) 5. 186. 1-8. [See Prājāpatya1 from which Prasvāpa is different]
प्राजापत्य: prājāpatya1 nt.: A missile of Prajāpati. (1) It was used by Bhīṣma and Arjuna against each other during the cattle-raid 4. 59. 21; (2) Employed by Droṇa, along with Aindra, against Yudhiṣṭhira to kill him (जिघांसुः); both missiles were repelled by Yudhiṣṭhira with Māhendrāstra 7. 132. 31-32. [See Prasvāpa which, although प्राजापत्य, is different from this missile].
Prājāpatya2 adj.: of the missile Pras-vāpa belonging to Prajāpati 5. 184. 12. [Different from Prājāpatya missile. See Prasvāpa and Prājāpatya1]

Prājāpatya2 nt.: Name of an asterism. Among the bad omens pointed out by Karṇa to Kṛṣṇa one was related to the lustrous, sharp planet Śanaiścara afflicting the Prājāpatya नक्षत्र (= Rohiṇī?) while simultaneously afflicting living beings all the more (प्राजापत्यं हि नक्ष्त्रं ग्रहस् तीक्ष्णो महाद्युतिः । शनैश्चरः पीडयति पीडयन् प्राणिनो ऽधिकम्) 5. 141. 7 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 5. 143. 8: प्राजापत्यं रोहिणीनक्षत्रम् । प्रजानां पतिर् दुर्यो-धनस् तदीयं नाम नक्षत्रम् उत्तरा-भाद्रपदाख्यम् इति वा । तेन पत्युः पीडया प्राणिनाम् अपि पीडेति युक्तम् । यद् वा पृथ्वीकूर्मोदरस्थां रोहिणीम् शनैश्चरः पीडयति तेन मध्यदेशे महान् क्षयो राज्ञो नाशश् चेति भावः । )
पञ्चेन्द्राणाम्: Pañcendrāṇām upākhyānam: Name of an Upākhyāna occurring in the पर्वन् called Pāñcālyāḥ svayaṃvaram. Described as wonderful (पञ्चेन्द्रा-णाम् उपाख्यानम् अत्रैवाद्भुतम् उच्यते) 1. 2. 87; it comprises the अध्याय 1. 189 (Pañcendropākhyāna).
पर्वसंग्रह: Parvasaṃgraha1 m.: Collection of a hundred sub-पर्वन्स् of the Bhārata 1. 2. 33-70. The number of these sub-पर्वन्स् is hundred (including the Harivaṃśa parvan and the Bhaviṣyat parvan called as the खिलस्) and it is supposed to have been made by Vyāsa himself (एतत् पर्वशतं पूर्णं व्यासेनोक्तं महात्मना) 1. 2. 70; it was then exactly repeated by Lomaharṣaṇin (Ugraśravas) 1. 2. 70; the collection of the sub-पर्वन्स् and the listing of the main events in each sub-पर्वन्स् which make up the major eighteen पर्वन्स् (1. 2. 72-233) consti-tute the summary of the Bhārata (समासो भारतस्यायं तत्रोक्तः पर्वसंग्रहः) 1. 2. 71, (एतद् अखिलम् आख्यातं भारतं पर्वसंग्रहात्) 1. 2. 234.

Parvasaṃgraha2 m.: Name of the 2nd पर्वन् in the list of a hundred sub-पर्वन्स् of the Bhārata supposed to have been made by Vyāsa in the Parvasaṃgraha 1. 2. 34, 33, 70, 243. It constitutes the second अध्याय of the Ādiparvan in which the sub-पर्वन्स् are listed (1. 2. 34-70) and the contents of the 18 major पर्वन्स् are summarized (1. 2. 71-234); thus the Parvasaṃgraha forms the layout of the grand narrative of the Mahā-bhārata (आख्यानं तद् इदम् अनुत्तमं महार्थम् विन्यस्तं महद् इह पर्व-संग्रहेण) 1. 2. 243; if one first listens to this summary of the contents, it becomes easy for him to go through the Bhārata as one can easily float over the extensive ocean with a small boat 1. 2. 243.
पाञ्चाल्याः: Pāñcālyāḥ svayaṃvaram: Name of the 12th पर्वन् in the list of a hundred sub-पर्वन्स् of the Bhārata supposed to have been made by Vyāsa in the Parvasaṃgraha (ततः स्वयंवरं देव्याः पाञ्चाल्याः पर्व चोच्यते) 1. 2. 36, 33, 70. In this पर्वन् Draupadī was won follow-ing the क्षत्रधर्म 1. 2. 37; it is referred to in the summary of the contents of the Ādiparvan where it is said that it contains the wonderful Pañcendra upākhyāna, Drupada's deliberation on the wedding of five (brothers) with one woman, and Draupadī's unusual marriage ordained by the gods (पञ्चेन्द्रा-णाम् उपाख्यानम् अत्रैवाद्भुतम् उच्यते ॥ पञ्चानाम् एकपत्नीत्वे विमर्शो द्रुपदस्य च । द्रौपद्या देवविहितो विवाहश् चाप्य् अमानुषः ॥ ) 1. 2. 87-88; referred to by Dhṛtarāṣṭra in his summary of the events made for Saṃjaya 1. 1. 102, and by Vaiśaṃ-pāyana in his summary made for Janame-jaya 1. 55. 22; related to the अध्यायस् 1. 174-189 (Draupadīsvayaṃvaraparvan).
पुत्रदर्शन: Putradarśana nt.: Name of the 94th पर्वन् of the Bhārata supposed to have been made by Vyāsa in the Parvasaṃgraha 1. 2. 67, 33, 70. The incident is mentioned while narrating the contents of the Āśramavāsaparvan; Dhṛtarāṣṭra, by the grace of Vyāsa, saw for a while the miracle of the return of his sons, grandsons, and other kings who were killed in the battle 1. 2. 214-215; it is related to the अध्यायस् 15. 36-44.
पुरुषसूक्त: Puruṣasūkta nt.: Name of a section (अध्यायस् 12. 338-339) in the Śāntiparvan 12. 338. 5 (perhaps part of the Nārāyaṇīya since the Puruṣa, also called पुरुषः विराट् 12. 338. 21, is identified with Nārāyaṇa 12. 339. 14). Vaiśaṃpāyana narrated it to Janamejaya when the latter asked him: “Who is the foremost Puruṣa and who is the source (of the universe) ? (को ह्य् अत्र पुरुषः श्रेष्ठः को वा योनिर् इहोच्यते) 12. 338. 1; Vaiśaṃ-pāyana narrated it to Janamejaya by the favour of his teacher Vyāsa to whom he paid obeisance 12. 338. 7, 4; the Puruṣasūkta is known in the Vedas as ऋत and सत्य 12. 338. 5; Vyāsa, the best among the sages (ऋषिसिंह 12. 338. 5), has summarized in it what the sages Kapila and others have ex-pounded in their शास्त्रस् 12. 338. 6-7; origi-nally the Puruṣottama (12. 338. 23) was described by the four-faced Brahman to his three-eyed son Rudra, hence called an old Itihāsa (इतिहासं पुरातनम्) 12. 338. 8-25; 12. 339. 1-21.
पूरोर्: Pūror vaṃśaḥ: Name (?) of a section of the sub-पर्वन् called Saṃbhavaparvan 1. 90. 96. It comprises the अध्यायस् 1. 89-90 in which Vaiśaṃpāyana, at the request of Jana-mejaya (1. 90. 1), informed him about the kings born in the family of Pūru; one who listens to this Pūruvaṃśa is released of all sins 1. 90. 96.
पैतामहशास्त्र: Paitāmahaśāstra nt.: Characterization of a नीतिशास्त्र (12. 59. 74) originally com posed by Lokapitāmaha (Brahmadeva) 12. 59. 29, 23. Described as auspicious (शुभ) 12. 59. 75; originally it consisted of one hundred thousand अध्यायस् 12. 59. 29; it was com-posed by Brahmadeva to allay the fear of gods who complained to him about the destru-ction of ब्रह्मन् and धर्म in the world due to which gods became equal of men (ब्रह्-मणश् च प्रणाशेन धर्मो ऽप्य् अनशद् ईश्वर । ततः स्म समतां याता मर्त्यैश् त्रिभुवनेश्वर) 12. 59. 25. 22-24; its contents are detailed in 12. 59. 29-74; 80-85; it was composed for the benefit of the world and for the establishment of the त्रिवर्ग (i. e. धर्म अर्थ and काम 12. 59. 29-30) 12. 59. 76; along with दण्डनीति, it would protect the world 12. 59. 77-79; it was first taught to Śaṅkara who abridged it to ten thousand अध्यायस् called Vaiśālākṣa 12. 59. 86-88. [See Barhas-patya, Bāhudantaka, Vaiśālākṣa]
पौलोम: Pauloma nt.: Name of the 4th पर्वन् in the list of a hundred sub-पर्वन्स् of the Bhārata supposed to have been made by Vyāsa in the Parvasaṃgraha 1. 2. 34, 33, 70. In the Pauloma parvan is narrated the extension of the lineage of Bhṛgu (भृगुवं-शस्य विस्तारः) from Bhṛgu to Śunaka 1. 2. 72; 1. 5. 7-8; 1. 8. 1-2; Sūta Ugraśravas is supposed to say that he would narrate the Pauloma Ākhyāna immediately after the beginning (यत् तु शौनकसत्रे ते भारता-ख्यानविस्तरम् । आख्यास्ये तत्र पौलोमम् आख्यानं चादितः परम्) 1. 2. 29 [this statement apparently refers to the occurrence of the Pauloma parvan (अध्यायस् 1. 4-12) in the present text of the Mahābhārata where at the beginning of the अध्याय 1. 4 the words लोमहर्षणपुत्र उग्रश्रवाः etc. occurring at 1. 1 are repeated; आदितः परम् seems to mean ‘from the beginning onwards’; V. S. Sukthankar, however, renders the line आख्यास्ये etc. as ‘then shall I narrate, to begin with, the excellent story of Pauloma’ ABORI 11. 183 (1930) = Sukthankar Memo-rial Edition I. 219 (1944)]; the Pauloma parvan comprises the अध्यायस् 1. 4-12.

Pauloma nt.: Name of a तीर्थ। A. Location: One of the five तीर्थस् on the southern ocean (समुद्रे तीर्थानि दक्षिणे) 1. 208. 1. B. Description: Very purifying (सुपावन) 1. 208. 3; all the five तीर्थस् there are described as very holy (सु-पुण्यानि) and adorned by ascetics (शोभितानि तपस्विभिः) 1. 208. 1. C. History: All these five तीर्थस् were once thronged by ascetics but later avoided by them as some of the ascetics were dragged away by five crocodiles who came to live there; then these तीर्थस् became desolate 1. 208. 2, 4-6. D. Epic event: Arjuna visited the तीर्थस् and freed them of the crocodiles 1. 208. 7-21; 1. 209. 1-23. [See Nārītīrthāni]
पौष्य: Pauṣya nt.: Name of the 3rd पर्वन् in the list of a hundred sub-पर्वन्स् of the Bhārata supposed to have been made by Vyāsa in the Parvasaṃgraha 1. 2. 34, 33, 70; It describes the greatness of Uttaṅka (माहात्म्यम् उत्तङ्कस्योपवर्णितम्) 1. 2. 72; related to the अध्याय 1. 3.

Pauṣya adj.: (of a योग) related to the नक्षत्र Puṣya. The sage Vyāsa asked first Yudhiṣṭhira to hold the hand (in marriage) of Kṛṣṇā since that was an auspicious day when the moon was going to have the Pauṣya yoga i. e. be in conjunction with Puṣya (अद्य पुण्या-हम् उत पाण्डवेय । अद्य पौष्यं योगम् उपैति चन्द्रमाः) 1. 190. 5 (Nī., however, on Bom. Ed. 1. 198. 5: पौष्यं पुष्यत्य् अनेनेति तं न तु पुष्यं तस्यावैवाहिक-त्वात्). [See Puṣya]
प्रजागर: Prajāgara nt.: Name of the 51st पर्वन् in the list of a hundred sub-पर्वन्स् of the Bhārata supposed to have been made by Vyāsa in the Parvasaṃgraha 1. 2. 50. It was occasioned by the anxiety of Dhṛtarāṣṭra (धृतराष्ट्रस्य चिन्तया) 1. 2. 50; Dhṛṭarāṣṭra was worried and lost sleep when he heard that the Pāṇḍavas would be led by Vāsudeva (Kṛṣṇa) (श्रुत्वा च पाण्डवान् यत्र वासुदेवपुरोगमान् । प्र-जागरः संप्रजज्ञे धृतराष्ट्रस्य चिन्-तया) 1. 2. 141; (5. 33. 6); in this पर्वन् Vidura gives all sort of beneficial advice to Dhṛtarāṣṭra (वाक्यानि विचित्राणि हितानि च) 1. 2. 142; alluded to in Dhṛtarāṣṭra's summary of the events made for Saṃjaya 1. 1. 118; the पर्वन् comprises the अध्यायस् 5. 33-41.
प्रतिज्ञापर्वन्: Pratijñāparvan nt.: Name of the 68th पर्वन् in the list of a hundred sub-पर्वन्स् of the Bhārata supposed to have been made by Vyāsa in the Parvasaṃgraha 1. 2. 57, 33, 70. The event of प्रतिज्ञा (Arjuna's vow to kill Jayadratha) referred to in the sum-mary of events made by Dhṛtarāṣṭra for Saṃjaya 1. 1. 134-135; related to the Adhyāyas 7. 52-60.
पुनर्वसु: Punarvasu m. (sg., du.): Name of a नक्षत्र। A. Religious rites: (1) Gifts under this नक्षत्र: Nārada told Devakī (13. 63. 2-4) that if one gave as gifts cakes (अपूपान्) and food (अन्नानि) under Punar-vasu (पुनर्वसौ) one obtained fame and good look and was born in a family that had ample food (बह्वन्ने जायते कुले) 13. 63. 9; (2) श्राद्ध: Yama told Śaśabindu (13. 89. 1) that if one offered a काम्य श्राद्ध under Punarvasu he reaped (ample) harvest (कृषिभागी भवेन् मर्त्यः कुर्वञ् श्राद्-धं पुनर्वसौ) 13. 89. 4. B. Smile: The two Pāñcāla warriors (Candradeva and Daṇḍadhara cf. the various readings under 8. 33. 15) guarding the wheels of Yudhiṣṭhira shone on his two sides as do the two Punar-vasu stars seen on the two sides of the moon (रथाभ्याशे चकासेते चन्द्रस्येव पुनर्-वसू) 8. 33. 16.
पुष्य: Puṣya1 m.: Name of a नक्षत्र, and of the moon's conjunction with this नक्षत्र (Puṣyayoga); also called Tiṣya (3. 188. 87). A. Description: auspicious (पुण्य-योग) 3. 261. 15. B. Considered favour-able for marching out of the army or for going out on a pilgrimage: (1) Duryodhana urged again and again the assembled kings to march towards Kurukṣetra on that very day since it was presided over by the Puṣya नक्षत्र (आज्ञापयच् च राज्ञस् तान् पार्थि-वान् दुष्टचेतसः । प्रयाध्वं वै कुरु-क्षेत्रं पुष्यो ऽद्येति पुनः पुनः) 5. 148. 3 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 3. 150. 3: पुष्यनक्-षत्रं हि अश्विन्याः पौरणमास्या उपरि अष्टम्यां भवति; cf. 5. 140. 18: सप्तमाच् चापि दिवसाद् अमावास्या भविष्यति); (2) Kṛṣṇa too, with the Pāṇḍavas, started towards Kuru (kṣetra) when Rauhiṇeya (Balarāma) went away on the day which was presided over by Puṣya (पुष्येण) 9. 34. 14; 9. 34. 9; (3) When the Mārgaśīrṣī (full moon day of the month Mārgaśīrṣa) had passed and the Puṣya had set in, the Pāṇḍa-vas, together with Dhaumya and other ascetics, started from the Kāmyaka forest towards the east (3. 91. 28) to visit the तीर्थस् (मार्गशीर्ष्याम् अतीतायां पुष्येण प्रययुस् तदा) 3. 91. 25; (4) Balarāma started for his तीर्थयात्रा under the Puṣya and returned to Kurukṣetra under the Śravaṇa; he was out for 42 days (चत्वारिंशद् अहान्य् अद्य द्वे च मे निःसृतस्य वै । पुष्येण सं-प्रयातो ऽस्मि श्रवणे पुनर् आगतः) 9 33. 5 (see Editor's note on the stanza, Cr. Ed. Vol. 11, p. 489); 9. 34. 14; (5) Drupada asked his Purohita, whom he sent as his mes-senger to the Kauravas, to start when the moon was in conjunction with the Puṣya so that he might achieve the objective of Yudhi-ṣṭhira (स भवान् पुष्ययोगेन … कौरवेयान् प्रयात्व् आशु कौन्तेयस्यार्थसिद्धये) 5. 6. 17; (6) Daśaratha asked his Purohita to make the necessary preparations in connec-tion with the consecration of Rāma as hair-apparent since on that night Puṣya was to enter into the auspicious conjunction (with the moon) (अद्य पुष्यो निशि ब्रह्मन् पुण्यं योगम् उपैष्यति) 3. 261. 15. C. Advent of the Kṛta Yuga: When the moon, the sun, the Tiṣya and the Bṛhaspati will come in one राशि, the Kṛta Yuga will commence (यदा चन्द्रश् च सूर्यश् च तथा तिष्य-बृहस्पती । एकराशौ समेष्यन्ति प्रपत्-स्यति तदा कृतम् ॥ ) 3. 188. 87 (Nī., how-ever, on Bom. Ed. 3. 190. 90: गुरुसूर्य-चन्द्राः यदा युगपत् पुष्यनक्षत्रम् एष्यन्ति तदा कृतयुगप्रवृत्तिर् इत्य् अर्थः). D. Religious rites: (1) Gifts under this नक्षत्र: Nārada told Devakī (13. 63. 2-4) that by giving gold, whether wrought or unwrought, as gift under Puṣya (पुष्ये) one shone like Soma (i. e. moon ?) in the worlds which have no (other) light (अनालो-केषु लोकेषु सोमवत् स विराजते) 13. 63. 10 (Nī. on Bom. Ed. 13. 64. 10: अनालोकेषु आलोकान्तरवर्जितेषु स्वयंप्रकाशेष्व् इत्य् अर्थः); (2) श्राद्ध: Yama told Śaśabindu (13. 89. 1) that one who desired prosperity should think of offering a काम्य श्राद्ध under the Puṣya नक्षत्र (पुष्टिकामो ऽथ पुष्येण श्राद्धम् ईहेत मानवः) 13. 89. 4. E. Bad omen: Among the bad omens for the Kauravas, pointed out by Vyāsa to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, one was related to a fierce comet (Rāhu ?) that had taken hold of Puṣya (धूमकेतुर् महाघोरः पुष्यम् आक्रम्य तिष्ठति) 6. 3. 12. [See Dhūmaketu, Pauṣya]
पूर्वा: Pūrvā Proṣṭhapadā f.: See Pūrvā Bhādrapadā.

Pūrvā Phalgunī f. (du., pl.): Name of a double नक्षत्र distinguished as Pūrvā and Uttarā. [Referred to also simply as Phalgunī 13. 89. 6]. A. Epic event: Arjuna was born on mountain Himavant under the junction of the two constellations Pūrvā Phalgunī and Uttarā Phalgunī and hence he was called Phalguna (उत्तराभ्यां च पूर्वाभ्यां फल्गुनीभ्याम् अहं दिवा । जातो … तेन मां फल्गुनं विदुः) 4. 39. 14 (Nī., who reads (Bom. Ed. 4. 44. 16) उत्तराभ्यां फलगुनीभ्यां नक्षत्राभ्याम् explains it as नक्षत्राभ्यां ताराभ्यां तत्र स्थिते चन्द्रे इत्य् अर्थः). B. Religious rites: (1) दान: Nārada told Devakī (13. 63. 2-4) that if one, after observing fast, gave to Brāh-maṇas under Pūrvā Phalgunī (फल्गुनी-पूर्वसमये) food mixed with condensed sugar cane juice (भक्षान् फाणितसंयुक्-तान्), one obtained prosperity (सौभाग्यम् ऋच्छति) 13. 63. 13; (2) श्राद्ध: Yama told Śaśabindu (13. 89. 1) that if one offered a काम्य श्राद्ध under (Pūrvā) Phalgunī one became prosperous (फल्गुनीषु ददच् छ्राद्धं सुभगः श्राद्धदो भवेत्) 13. 89. 6.

Pūrvā Bhādrapadā f.; also called Pūrvā Proṣṭhapadā (du., pl.); Pūrva Pro-ṣṭhapada m. (sg.) (6. 3. 14): Name of a double नक्षत्र distinguished as Pūrvā and Uttarā. A. Religious rites: (1) दान: Nārada told Devakī (13. 63. 2-4) that by offering the राजमाषस् (kind of beans) as a gift under the Pūrvabhādrapadā conjunction one enjoys all kinds of food and becomes happy in next life (पूर्वभाद्रपदायोगे राजमाषान् प्र-दाय तु । सर्वभक्षफलोपेतः स वै प्रेत्य सुखी भवेत् ॥ ) 13. 63. 31; (2) श्राद्ध: Yama told Śaśabindu (13. 89. 1) that by offering a काम्य श्राद्ध under Pūrvaproṣṭhapadā one obtained many goats and sheep (पूर्वप्रोष्ठपदाः कुर्वन् बहु विन्देद् अजाविकम्) 13. 89. 13; but in general one is not supposed to offer any rites to gods and manes under the two Proṣṭhapadā नक्षत्रस् (दैवं पित्र्यम् अथापि च । … न प्रोष्ठपदयोः कार्यम्) 13. 107. 119. B. Bad effect: Śukra, when in conjunction with the two Proṣṭhapadās has always wealth, so also the Lord of riches (i. e. Kubera); Śukra (when in conjunction with the two नक्षत्रस्) takes away from men what-ever wealth they had earned as desired (नित्यं प्रोष्ठपदाभ्यां च शुक्रे धनपतौ तथा । मनुष्येभ्यः समा-दत्ते शुक्रश् चित्तार्जितं धनम् ॥ ) 5. 112. 3 (Nī., however, on Bom. Ed. 5. 114. 3: प्रोष्ठपदाभ्याम् इति तृतीया … सप्तम्यर्थे तेन तस्मिन् नक्षत्रद्वये शुक्रे शुक्रवा-सरे तद्योगे सति शुक्रो ऽग्निः धनपतौ कुबेरस्य वृद्ध्यर्थं मनुष्येभ्यः संप्रदानेभ्यः धनं दत्ते ददाति । शुक्रश् चित्तार्जितम् इत्य् अनेन वह्निरेतस्-त्वं तस्य प्रदर्श्यते । धनार्थी उक्तन-क्षत्रवारयोगे वह्निं प्रार्थयेत् । तच् च धनं यागादिद्वारा वा भूमौ निखनेन वा सर्वं कुबेरं प्रत्य् एव गच्छतीति भावः). C. Bad omen: Among the bad omens pointed out by Vyāsa to Dhṛtarā-ṣṭra one referred to Śukra's having ascended the Pūrva Proṣṭhapada constellation and then having gone over to the Uttara Proṣṭhapada, was still looking at it (i. e. looking at the Pūrva Proṣṭhapada) 6. 3. 14 (for the citation and Nī.'s commentary on it see above Uttarā Bhādrapadā p. 232. 2). [See Uttarā Bhādrapadā]
पूर्वाषाढा: Pūrvāṣāḍhā f. (pl.): Name of a double नक्षत्र distinguished as Pūrvā and Uttarā. Religious rites: (1) दान: Nārada told Devakī (13. 63. 2-4) that if one, after observing fast, gave as a gift under the Pūrvāṣāḍhā (पूर्वास्व् अषाढासु) pots full of curds (दधिपात्राणि) to a Brāhmaṇa born in good family and of good conduct and who was proficient in the Vedas, the giver, after death, was born in a family that was rich in cows 13. 63. 25; (2) श्राद्ध: Yama told Śaśabindu (13. 89. 1) that by offering a काम्य श्राद्ध under the Pūrvāṣāḍhā (the word पूर्वा does not occur but is easily inferred) one obtained excellent fame (यशो ऽषाढास्व् अनुत्तमम्) 13. 89. 10.
पौष: Pauṣa m.: Name of a month Aṅgiras had told Bhīṣma that if one spent the month of Pauṣa eating only once a day (भक्तेनैकेन यः क्षपेत्) he was born fortunate, handsome and famous 13. 109. 19.
प्रोष्ठपदा: Proṣṭhapadā: See Pūrvā Bhādrapadā and Uttarā Bhādrapadā.
प्रौष्ठपद: Prauṣṭhapada m.: Name of the month Bhādrapada. Aṅgiras had told Bhīṣma (13. 109. 9) that one who spent the month of Prauṣṭha-pada taking food only once a day obtained rich, prosperous and steady power (प्रौष्ठ-पदं तु यो मासम् एकाहारो भवेन् नरः । धनाढ्यं स्फीतम् अचलम् ऐश्वर्यं प्रतिपद्यते) 13. 109. 27.
पञ्चनद: Pañcanada nt.: Name of a place marked by five rivers ? (identical with Pañca-srotas ?) Described as famous in the world and holy (लोके ख्यातं पञ्चनदं च पुण्यम्) 3. 134. 11 (Nī., however, on Bom. Ed. 3. 134. 12: लोके ऽपि पञ्चानां विषयस्रोतसां समाहारः पञ्चनदम् उपेयम्). [See Pañca nadyaḥ and Pañcasrotas below, and Pañcanada in Section 1. 5 A]

Pañcanada m. (pl.), nt. (sg.): Name of a country and its people. A. Location: West of Hāstinapura 2. 23. 10; 2. 29. 1; between the western ocean and the Gāndhāra 14. 84. 17; on way from Hāstinapura to Dvārakā 16. 8. 43 (see below Epic events No. 1, 5, 6, and S. K. Belvalkar's Critical Notes to Mausala Parvan Vol. 19, pp. 48-49). B. Descrip-tion: Brave (शूर) 6. 20. 10; croocked (जिह्म) 8. 30. 62. C.
